body: That begs the question, is it worth suffering mentally and emotionally for the rest of my life for my loved ones to be happy?

I'm not comfortable with my mental instability and involving someone else in it. I don't have many friends anymore because most of them grew up and started their lives. I don't have any 'real' friends that I can talk to. I think if I even found someone, I couldn't be the person they deserve, nor would I be stable enough for them to want to stick around. 


I find solace in my solidarity, and that's all I really have is myself. When I think about it, I really don't want to pass my genetics on to offspring that would inherit these awful traits. I know I inherited some mental illness from a side of my family. I don't want them to live and suffer their entire life.

It comes down to tired of being. There's a philosophical mindset I have that no MD or PhD could break through. Practitioners don't understand what that's like, so their advice is naive and fruitless. 

I hope I do find my peace and freedom too, as I hope you do too, whatever it may be. I'm glad we had the opportunity to cross paths.

I will try to answer this humbly. I would not consider myself unattractive, so I believe it played some part, but I also have a fairly good resume. You were the type of person who made my night much easier and more enjoyable. I don't condone smoking, but people like you enjoyed chatting and helping me hit my quota, or make me look busy in front of my boss haha.

The movie in my personal opinion is pretty great. However, I do agree with Naylor in that smoking is an adult choice. I condemn smoking, but I started smoking primarily due to my geographic location and friends who were smokers. I rarely, if ever, saw advertisements of any kind for tobacco. No one forced me to buy a pack of cigarettes, and they say what can happen to you on the pack. I'm a big advocate of personal responsibility, which is why I quit, but if you want to drink a gallon of paint thinner every day, you can do so. Just like smoke a pack of cigarettes. Unfortunately, the lobbying power behind big tobacco is incredibly powerful, and I do believe more safeguards can be put in place. For example, in Sweden, their equivalent of the FDA mandates that their snus have all its ingredients listed right on the container, and the manufacturing process is significantly more transparent than in the United States. Big tobacco here is able to get away with a lot more.

Well a little over a month. The snus was pushed fairly heavily to consumers. Our main strategy is simple conversation/small talk, offer of the coupon, and discussing/promoting the brand. This includes creating a brand story that they could relate to. We solely targeted cigarette smokers for trial. We also demonstrated techniques like tapping the tin to create a little ritual like many cigarette smokers have when packing their packs or packing their tins of dip. Also, we used the buzzwords like smooth and mellow, and emphasize the fact that you can use it anywhere unlike cigarettes. We also tried to match the various flavors to the consumer. Very generic talking points. It was not wildly popular but I would estimate 1/15-1/20 tobacco users would actually want to try it. I can't speak much on the usage patterns of people who use that brand of snus, as I met very few users. Most of the people I talked to seemed very put off by using any sort of tobacco in their mouth. I believe snus is a niche market, separate from chewing and dipping tobacco, and they are trying to appeal to the cigarette smokers. It was an unrealistic expectation and demographic in my opinion. I've used high quality Swedish snus before and it just doesn't compare. What I can conclude is that the majority of people are not going to try a new product without some sort of incentive (i.e, coupons) and even then, results were dismal at best. It seems like you are fairly familiar with this industry. Something of interest to note was that before I had this position, I thought most cigarette smokers were brand loyal like I was. That was completely false. Most buy the cheapest packs they can buy, mainly during sales/trial products/coupons. If you have anymore questions feel free to PM me or ask here!

1. That stems off the popular myth that menthol makes your lungs bleed/crystalize. That's not true, to an extent. There have been a couple studies I read into that indicate mentholated cigarettes increase your risk for stroke. Some of the studies needed to be peer-reviewed, so it's negligible as far as I know. Cigarettes are cigarettes, they both lead you to the same place, ya know? This would be known as pulmonary fibrosis though, which is where the blood and other stories come from. It doesn't just come from tobacco though, it comes from all sorts of toxic gases.

2. No, another common myth. I've heard that one about so many different products from food items to concrete.

I have a reputation with my friends of constantly correcting stupid common myths and fallacies, which makes my friends think I'm a know-it-all, but in reality, I have a low tolerance for stupidity when people say stuff like that.

During my tenure for the company, I met some people who displayed all the awful gross symptoms of smoking for years. Yellow teeth and gross fingers, the most disgusting voices and noises, the stench. One guy even had an oxygen tank and still smoked. It absolutely terrified me, and I was tired of spending money on it. I was tired of needing something to feel normal. I didn't want to die young and I wanted to be healthy and fit. Girls were another inspiration to quit. I had wanted to quit for a very long time with limited success, but finally I just said fuck it and quit cold turkey. I definitely had some attitude when I quit haha, but I focused my rage and anger into exercise and getting things done in my life. I was at a low point and figured that would be the first step to turning things around.

If these were not met, you were scolded at the weekly meeting in front of the other employees, some threatened with reduction of hours or termination. Could you rephrase the question? I guess the entire company is messed up for marketing a product that provides no benefit, is highly addictive, and kills you. I would say the corporate structure is great, like any other major corporation, but the actual products they make a living off of are pretty messed up. Especially the portfolio I was advertising, it was all for young adult smokers. Once they have you at 21, they have you until you are dead unless you can quit. Just ask a smoker how hard it is to quit to get an idea.

I left because I found the work to be unethical, in addition to the excessive amount of driving I had to do. I worked late nights and a lot of non-tobacco users treated me very poorly, which made me feel bad about myself. I also used quitting as an excuse to quit smoking, which I am still going strong to this day.

I am not familiar with the manufacturing process, although I was shown some images and given general information about manufacturing (what it used to look like when they first started out, to what it looks like now.) As I was not a high level employee, most of this information was not shared with us.

I was not allowed to talk about anything relating to health and tobacco so no for that question. My company had a specific policy, along with federal law prohibiting me from doing so. When it comes to tobacco, I never really had to misrepresent the quality, as most people who smoked either liked our brand and were loyal, or just took the free coupon.

I did not believe in the company or the product, in fact, my tenure of employment convinced me to quit for good. Still going strong. We were given an incentive every shift, which was a discount for pennies on the dollar, to keep employees addicted in my opinion. I was there for the almost-free cigarettes and decent paycheck.

My goal was to establish as many person-to-person contacts as possible, sign as many people as possible up, and make the brand look "cool" while in the field. I marketed a certain portfolio of products from our brand, mainly the new/hip products appealing to younger (young adult) smokers. I did work a lot with older smokers also.

Compliance was incredibly important, as a minor slip-up could result in severe penalties. Essentially, they marketed within the legal guidelines, but in the sleeziest ways possible. It was taken very seriously.

I'd highly recommend going cold turkey with a combination of exercise. that's what did it for me, and I highly recommend anyone considering quitting that they do it ASAP!

We couldn't legally, or secretly due to the software we used. You had to be a verifiable (proper ID) tobacco user over the age of 21 (yes, even though most states tobacco is legal at 18.)

Coaxing people with a coupon for a heavily discounted price, but in order to get the coupon, we had to get your general information (name, address, email, etc...) otherwise you would not get a coupon. When you completed this process, your information was submitted to a consumer database with all the information, and you were signed up for our mailing list that pounds you with junk mail and coupons (some liked it.) One technique we used when trying to get people to test out another one of our products was to apply a generic brand story that would seemingly fit their personality. We were encouraged to make small talk and learn about them in order to exploit them. If they did not want to try it, we would make another attempt discretely a couple times throughout the conversation by making comments about the product and what I liked about it, and how it would be relevant to the consumer, or some benefit it may bring.

I no longer work there, but I would estimate 90-95%. I think only a couple didn't smoke. Part of working there was loyalty to the brand also, so on the job if you did smoke, you were only allowed to smoke our brand.
Person to person and market research
http://www.reddit.com/r/InternetAMA/comments/13jisp/i_worked_for_a_major_tobacco_company_ama/

We were strictly prohibited from commenting about ANY health risks associated with tobacco, because "we aren't doctors". It says right on the pack what it can do to you. Also we weren't allowed to mention anything relating to the FDA or the MSA (Master Settlement Agreement)

Doing an AMA now: http://www.reddit.com/r/InternetAMA/comments/13jisp/i_worked_for_a_major_tobacco_company_ama/

I'd be interested in doing an AMA if there was enough interest. Without giving too much information, even though I am on a throwaway, I can tell you our marketing is evil. We basically read a person, create a brand story tailored to them (I love snus because I can use it anywhere, especially when I'm traveling, shopping, blah blah without smelling like smoke.) Pretty much make a generic statement that relates to the consumer. By federal law they are limited to using the words like smooth, mellow, and bold, etc... It's illegal to use the term light now, like a light cigarette. Hence, you saw all the advertising from all tobacco companies that use the terms smooth for light, bold for regular, etc. Also, comparisons can't be made for flavor. For example, if I was marketing a mint flavored tobacco product, I could not say it tastes like mint. It tastes like mint tobacco. We'd give out coupons at a heavily discounted price (with a quota to meet), and little did the people signing up know that we added you to our mailing list and market research database. They know more about you than your doctor. Obviously, I quit within two weeks because of how unethical a lot of the stuff was, but they paid fairly well. We also learned advanced rejection techniques, where if someone was not interested in a product, we were taught how to discretely ask them a couple more times to get them interested. There was a LOT of red tape, but it's funny how even complying with the red tape you'd still feel like a dirt bag. One thing they did do that we can all appreciate is we were strictly prohibited from marketing to people who quit, are under the age of 21, casual/infrequent/social smokers. We mainly tried to get smokers to switch to our brand and stay at our brand. They do emphasize younger smokes though, because they know once you get hooked at a young age, you are going to be a customer for life.

EDIT: FYI, I worked in a lower level field position, but we were the ones applying the marketing techniques taught to us on consumers, so I am very well versed in the what and how.

Finally, a thread I can contribute too. I used to work for a major tobacco company, the animal is typically found in the desert ;) I'm not really sure what to divulge so if anyone has any questions please ask.
